business.title: Personalized neoantigen-targeting cancer vaccines in ovarian cancer: a phase 1 trial
business.desc: Personalized neoantigen-targeting cancer vaccines in the adjuvant setting are of increasing interest across malignancies. Here we report the results of a phase 1 clinical trial testing the feasibility and safety of personalized neoantigen-targeting cancer vaccines for high-grade epithelial ovarian cancer. ‘NeoVax’ consisted of pools of synthetic long peptides targeting patient-specific neoantigens admixed with the immunostimulant poly-ICLC, was combined with delayed administration of anti-PD-1 antibody, and was tested in ten patients (one newly diagnosed patient (Cohort A) and nine patients at first recurrence (Cohort B)) with platinum-sensitive ovarian cancer following standard-of-care platinum doublet chemotherapy. Nine of 12 evaluable Cohort B patients were vaccinated (75%, 90% CI 47–93%) and 1 of 9 Cohort A patients (11%, 90% CI 0.6–43%). No unexpected safety signals were encountered and no patients discontinued treatment due to toxicity. Across patients, >70% selected targets remained detectable by noninvasive cell-free DNA analysis despite a median of 6.5 months from the time of diagnostic biopsy to vaccine administration, during which, patients received standard-of-care chemotherapy. Biomarker analysis was suggestive of biologic activity of the vaccine in six of ten patients and this was associated with broader tumor and vaccine-specific immune responses in blood and tumor following vaccination. Resistant tumor clones reflected diverse mechanisms affecting antigen presentation, indicative of immune-selective pressure exerted by vaccination. Overall, the interplay between the repertoire of antigens presented by the tumor and the breadth of induced immunity seemed to dictate clinical efficacy following vaccination. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT04024878 . A phase 1 trial shows that treatment of patients with high-grade serous ovarian cancer with personalized neoantigen vaccines combined with PD-1 blockade was feasible and led to tumor-specific immune responses in many patients and putative mechanisms of resistance related to antigen presentation were identified via cell-free DNA analysis.

technology.title: Symmetries and continuous attractors in disordered neural circuits
technology.desc: A core challenge in neuroscience is reconciling idealized models with experimental data. Classical continuous-attractor models describe neural representations of continuous variables such as head direction. Symmetry in the weights generates a manifold of stable states, with tuning curves identical up to shifts. Rodent head-direction cells, by contrast, are markedly heterogeneous. Such heterogeneity, we show, is nevertheless compatible with these models. Here we build, directly from head-direction cell data, recurrent networks that behave as quasicontinuous attractors. A generative process then reproduces the heterogeneous tuning of these cells while making connectivity and dynamics tractable at large N. Although the weights appear disordered, they carry a circular symmetry whose eigenvalue degeneracies could signify continuous-attractor organization in connectome data. Dynamical mean-field theory recovers the ingredients of classical ring attractors, namely, Mexican hat interactions and a spontaneously broken symmetry producing bump states. Continuous-attractor mechanisms may thus operate in complex mammalian circuits. Head-direction cells are far more disorderly than classical continuous-attractor models allow. Clark et al. show that this disorder is nevertheless compatible with these models and that the underlying connectivity matrix hides a circular symmetry.
